items.rss_title: Turning Volatility Into Value
items.rss_description: Turning Volatility Into Value Underwriting RyanMeyer Wed, 10/14/2026 - 10:37 Amid today's heightened uncertainty, Dawn Miller, chief commercial officer at Lloyd's, explores how insurers can innovate their way to value both for themselves and for their clients. October 14, 2026 Image Paul Carroll We’re in an exceptionally volatile period, with major geopolitical and economic risks on top of climate-driven catastrophes, nuclear verdicts, and more. The International Insurance Society’s annual Global Insurance Forum in November, which you’re sponsoring and hosting at Lloyd’s, has as its theme this year: "Turning Volatility Into Value." How do we do that? Dawn Miller I'm just coming off some time at CIAB [Council of Insurance Agents and Brokers] in Colorado, and the topic that is on everyone's mind, in addition to market conditions, is how multiple perils are intersecting with global trends to create an increasingly varied and complex risk landscape, with some risks well modeled and others less so. In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few. It’s the interaction among these different risks that is adding new layers of complexity. We have innovations that allow us to model with more transparency, and we can bring in supplementary models to assess risk. That's a good thing. But it takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today. Paul Carroll Yes, some people who’ve written for us refer to a “polycrisis.” You mention modeling. Is that the main way insurers make sense of all these complicated connections, or is it improvements in scenario planning, or something else? Dawn Miller I believe it's multiple things. We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role. The modeling itself is a bit of a Rubik's Cube with multiple facets to it. Paul Carroll Wall Street talks a lot about alpha and embraces volatility because it creates opportunities. Historically, insurers have not liked volatility. How do you change that thinking? Dawn Miller Given that Lloyd’s is guiding a marketplace, we're creating the conditions for success for the world's best risk takers to attach the risks they want to underwrite with capital. We see a mix in our marketplace. We do see investors coming in looking for some of that volatility. That’s what they like, and it fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist. Paul Carroll Volatility requires agility not just for those transacting in your marketplace but for you, too. How is Lloyd's getting faster at identifying opportunities and scaling the winners as quickly as possible? Dawn Miller In March, we launched our new five-year strategy, Advance and protect. It is designed to sharpen Lloyd’s financial edge and maximize our unique capital advantage, including by creating a more efficient and flexible marketplace by making the platform more investable, clear, transparent and agile. Right now, there's some additional reporting, different ways of working, maybe some duplicated oversight here and there—things that have grown up over time for all the right intentions, but maybe as we evolve are not as pragmatic any more. All of those cause a little bit of extra cost, whether it's in time or resources, because time is money at the end of the day. So we're making things much clearer, making it much more cost-efficient, making sure we are an engine for driving new talent into the marketplace, attracting the best talent and then recycling them back out as advocates and having the marketplace stronger for their being with us. You're creating an ecosystem that is the center of attracting the world's best risk takers, the best capital together with the best brokers, best clients, the best risk. What that gives us is the ability to innovate. When we think about Lloyd's and the underpinnings of our strategy, our superpower is our capital diversification benefits. Our other superpowers are around our license structure, the framework we have for innovation, the ability to syndicate risk rapidly, our very strong financial strength ratings. Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve. And we are the marketplace for that sort of solution creation. Paul Carroll At ITL, in our little way, our mantra is: Nobody is as smart as everybody. Dawn Miller That's exactly right. Our role is to convene a marketplace, creating those conditions for success. It happened 338 years ago when people came together over a cup of coffee and said, Let's share this risk so we can get these ships across the globe. Today, the same principle of combining expertise and capital continues across the underwriting room, Lloyd’s Lab and Lloyd’s Academy. Paul Carroll I’m glad you mentioned the lab and the academy, because, as an old hand on innovation efforts, I wanted to ask how they fit into your broader innovation ecosystem. Dawn Miller Absolutely. As you know, Lloyd's Lab launched in 2018 to make sure we had a place to accelerate—not necessarily incubate, and I want to make that distinction—new risk-taking ideas or risk-servicing ideas. Over time, we've grown to have about 160 alumni. This past cohort, Cohort 17, just went through a selection process. We received 280 applications from 31 countries. Fifteen companies were invited to pitch to the market, and 10 were selected for the 10-week Accelerator program. The market plays a central role in that selection process because the Lab is designed to respond to real market needs. The focus of Cohort 17 has been in areas where the Lloyd’s market is actively seeking solutions that improve how the market operates day to day to strengthen its ability to respond to the complexity of today’s risk landscape and this can be seen through the themes: operational efficiency, new products and experimental innovation. What does that mean? They come in at all different stages of businesses and ideas. They have mentors from the marketplace. They hone, shift, and massage their product and their service. Then they exit the other end, generally about 80 to 85% of them, with either capacity for a proof of concept or a service contract or service proof of concept into the marketplace. That ranges from new products—cloud downtime, wildfire, data analytics—to a whole variety of services. They work their way through the market, with an accelerated cover holder process. Some of them, like Parsyl, started in the Lloyd’s Lab. Parsyl began by using data and technology to tackle risks in global health supply chains, then became a Syndicate-in-a-Box and now has in-principle approval to become a full syndicate. That’s the process of taking innovation, testing and proving it in the market, and ultimately giving it the opportunity to scale. They're a part of our ecosystem once they come out as alumni, and they stay within our ecosystem around the world. We continue to help by giving them opportunities to be exposed to end clients, to regulators, to investors, etc. Paul Carroll How do you expect these topics—including innovation, geopolitical risk, and emerging technologies—to be developed at the Global Insurance Forum? Dawn Miller I always look forward to the Global Insurance Forum; it's a place where market leaders and market practitioners are coming together to exchange on an equal level. We’re reflecting the trends of the times, whether that’s private credit, scaling innovation or how we move beyond the tactical. This year’s theme, “Turning volatility into value,” really captures that. It’s about moving beyond reacting to uncertainty and using better insight, specialist expertise and flexible capital to anticipate changing needs, build solutions and give customers the confidence to invest and grow. The companies that come together are from all around the world. Everybody's lens is going to have a slightly different take on how they deal with geopolitical risk or how they're dealing with supply chain or how they're dealing with credit risk or what they're facing at that exact moment. Bringing all of that together allows us to create a narrative that firmly implants how our industry is driving resilience forward. Our industry provides the oxygen for the economies around us. And I believe we allow our industry to represent itself or be represented by others in a way other than that. I wish we talked more about the outcome our industry enables: resilience. We need to explain insurance through communities, businesses and economies it enables to recover and thrive and persist. The forum also creates a great opportunity to bring some of our young leaders to the table. Their perspectives are varied and rich, and we need that diversity of thought. Paul Carroll As someone who’s covered technology innovations for decades, I confess that it was only about 15 years ago that I realized that none of that happens without insurance. Every major innovation—the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, social media, search engines, GPS, the driverless car—comes with risks, and nobody can take those risks without some sort of protection. Dawn Miller Right. Isn't it funny? We all sort of take it for granted. If we could just reframe the conversation and talk more clearly about how insurance creates resilient communities, helping them thrive, we would give people a much better understanding of the value our industry provides. At Lloyd’s, we don’t just seek to understand risk, we take it on, bringing together expertise, capital and risk appetite to help businesses move forward. The issue couldn't be more important than it is right now, with the multiple layers of risks that surround us. Paul Carroll Thanks, Dawn. It’s always great talking with you. Dawn Miller Thank you for having me, Paul; always a pleasure. If you’re interested in attending the Global Insurance Forum, you can register here. Insurance Thought Leadership

items.title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.original_title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.rss_title: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation
items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.original_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_description: Finding Value in Today's Volatility PaulCarroll Mon, 10/19/2026 - 20:00 I don't know about you, but I'm a bit wary when I pick up my phone first thing in the morning and check on the state of the world. There's rioting where? A convective storm or wildfire destroyed what? The war in Ukraine or Iran took what turn? Inflation was how high, or job growth how low? And the volatility is building on itself, creating what some of our authors have dubbed the "polycrisis." Economic problems lead to rioting in France, which destabilizes the Western alliance, which emboldens Putin in Ukraine, which feeds the political crisis in the U.S., which.... The insurance industry generally dislikes volatility. Insurers want a decade or two of data on a risk so they can price it properly. But how do you understand risks that appear so suddenly and can interact in such complex ways? To get a sense, I turned to Dawn Miller, the chief commercial officer at Lloyd's and CEO of Lloyd's Americas, who explained how new data sources, better models, scenario planning and just generally processing information faster can at least help. Let's have a look. Here is the full interview I did with Dawn. And here is a link to this year's Global Insurance Forum, which our sister organization the International Insurance Society is holding at Lloyd's in London on Nov. 15 and 16 on the theme, "Turning Volatility Into Value." But I'll summarize: Dawn says, " We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role." She adds that some firms like at least some volatility because it creates more potential for upside and "fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role [at Lloyd's] is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist." Dawn cautions that today's environment is full of "new layers of complexity": "In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few.... I t takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today." But she's optimistic about the industry's ability to innovate, including through Lloyd's Lab and the Lloyd's Academy, to help the insurance industry react faster as perils develop and interact. She also sees the industry cooperating, including through the ecosystem that Lloyd's fosters: "Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve." When I wake up tomorrow morning, I'll still peek at my phone with one eye open to check on the state of the world, but all is not lost. I hope to see you in London so we can discuss the polycrisis and its many implications in person. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll New data sources, better models, scenario planning and faster processing of information can help insurers turn today's "polycrisis" into value for themselves and for customers. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist." Dawn cautions that today's environment is full of "new layers of complexity": "In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few.... I t takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today." But she's optimistic about the industry's ability to innovate, including through Lloyd's Lab and the Lloyd's Academy, to help the insurance industry react faster as perils develop and interact. She also sees the industry cooperating, including through the ecosystem that Lloyd's fosters: "Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve." When I wake up tomorrow morning, I'll still peek at my phone with one eye open to check on the state of the world, but all is not lost. I hope to see you in London so we can discuss the polycrisis and its many implications in person. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll New data sources, better models, scenario planning and faster processing of information can help insurers turn today's "polycrisis" into value for themselves and for customers. items.extracted_text: Gallagher Re estimates global insured cat losses at $92bn for 9M’26, lowest since 2019 - Artemis.bm Gallagher Re estimates global insured cat losses at $92bn for 9M’26, lowest since 2019 - Artemis.bm Gallagher Re estimates global insured cat losses at $92bn for 9M’26, lowest since 2019 21st October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Insured losses from natural catastrophe events across the globe during the first nine months of 2026 are estimated to have reached US $92 billion, representing the lowest total for the first nine months of a year since 2019, and 29% below the 10-year average of $128 billion, according to reinsurance broker Gallagher Re’s Q3 2026 Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report. At the same time, the broker noted that severe convective storms (SCS) generated at least $43 billion in insured losses in the United States alone during Q3 2026, while on a global basis, SCS accounted for nearly 60% of all insured catastrophe losses during the first three-quarters of the year. “The insurance industry has now experienced six consecutive quarters without a single natural catastrophe event generating more than USD10 billion in insured losses, representing one of the longest such stretches in decades,” Gallagher Re said. “Despite 54 billion-dollar economic loss events and 24 billion-dollar insured loss events globally, both broadly in line with historical averages, lower event severity has kept aggregate losses well below average,” the broker continued. The image below, taken from Gallagher Re’s latest report, highlights how 2026 continues to run below the 10-year average for both insured and economic losses, while the United States contributes 62% of global insured losses to-date in 2026. As mentioned, while catastrophe losses have remained subdued, severe convective storms (SCS) continued to dominate industry losses across the globe. According to Gallagher Re, in the US alone, insurers incurred at least $43 billion in SCS losses through Q3’26, marking a record fourth consecutive year in which annual insured losses from the peril have exceeded $40 billion. At the same time, Europe has also witnessed heavy SCS activity in recent months, recording at least $9 billion in SCS insured losses, including a $3.8 billion in losses from a late-August outbreak alone. Severe convective storms also accounted for nearly 60% of all insured catastrophe losses during the first three quarters of the year. Another image below taken from the broker’s report, showcases that a number of perils such as SCS are running above the ten-year average for insured losses so far in 2026. Gallagher Re also observed that hurricane activity also contributed to regional losses during the period. In the eastern Pacific, Hurricanes Lala, Lowell and Nolo all affected the Hawaiian Islands during the third quarter of 2026. Gallagher Re stated that Hurricane Lala was particularly impactful, noting that it passed close to the Big Island in mid-August and became Hawaii’s second weather-related disaster of the year to generate economic losses exceeding $1 billion. Meanwhile, in the Atlantic, Hurricane Isaias became the first major hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season before reaching Florida’s Panhandle on October 9th as a Category 2 storm. Gallagher Re importantly noted that because the hurricane occurred outside the nine-month reporting period, its losses were excluded from the broker’s $92 billion nine-month loss total. However, the broker has said that it expects the storm to generate insured losses in the low to mid-single-digit billions of US dollars. Despite the relatively low period of below average catastrophe losses recorded so far in 2026, Gallagher Re warned that this should not be interpreted as evidence of reduced underlying risk. “Alongside elevated secondary peril activity, 2026 has also been marked by the rapid emergence of what could become one of the strongest El Niño events on record,” the broker explained. “The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) projects a greater than 81% probability that El Niño will maintain a “very strong” status into January 2027. Forecasts suggest the event could peak during the fourth quarter before weakening during 2027, with the potential for a subsequent transition to La Niña conditions. For (re)insurers, such shifts can materially alter regional risk patterns, creating the need to reassess exposure concentrations, accumulations and capital deployment strategies,” Gallagher Re added. Gallagher Re’s report also highlighted historical evidence linking ENSO transition periods with meaningful changes in catastrophe activity. The broker said monitoring these developments would be important as the industry beings to prepare for the 2027 renewal season. Rising temperatures and prolonged drought were also identified as major themes of 2026. Gallagher Re stated that global temperatures during the first nine months of 2026 ranked as the second highest recorded for that period in the modern historical record, which extends back to at least 1850. Multiple countries, including France, the UK and the contiguous United States experienced their warmest summers on record for the June-to-August period. The resulting consequences included increased wildfire activity, agricultural losses, disruption to transport networks and a substantial rise in insurance claims linked to drought, particularly in France. Steve Bowen, Chief Science Officer at Gallagher Re, commented: “At first glance, 2026 appears to have been a relatively favorable year for the insurance industry. Global insured losses have remained below recent averages, largely because the industry has avoided a meaningful concentration of major loss events. We have now gone six consecutive quarters without a natural catastrophe generating more than USD10 billion in insured losses, an unusually long stretch by historical standards.” Bowen continued: “However, catastrophe activity and catastrophe losses are not necessarily the same thing. The world has still experienced a sizeable number of significant disasters in 2026, but relatively few have occurred in locations or under circumstances that generated outsized insured losses. Many of the costliest events instead produced substantial economic, humanitarian, and societal impacts, with much of the recovery ultimately falling on governments, businesses, and affected communities. “Looking ahead, the potential transition toward La Niña conditions in 2027 is a reminder of how quickly the catastrophe landscape can shift from one year to the next. Periods like this provide an opportunity to reassess exposures, accumulations, and portfolio resilience. items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. items.title: AI Shapes Customer Demand While Measuring It
items.original_title: AI Shapes Customer Demand While Measuring It
items.rss_title: AI Shapes Customer Demand While Measuring It
items.rss_description: AI Shapes Customer Demand While Measuring It AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Mon, 10/12/2026 - 14:13 AI systems now shape customer choices through recommendations and interactions, making causal identification essential to distinguish genuine needs from system-influenced demand. October 20, 2026 Image When companies talk about understanding customer needs, they often assume a simple path: Underlying Need → Observed Demand A customer has an underlying need, even if they cannot fully articulate it. Through questions, data, and observed behavior, companies try to work backward from what the customer says or chooses, to understand what that person actually needs. Demand discovery has therefore traditionally been treated as a process of finding something that already exists. In a previous article, I argued that reproducing an outcome is not the same as understanding the causal mechanism that produced it. The same distinction applies to customer demand: observing what customers choose is not the same as understanding why that choice emerged. What deserves more attention is the arrow in the middle. The path from underlying need to observed demand is never empty. What customers see, how they are questioned, what recommendations they receive, and how they interact with a system can all shape the demand that eventually becomes visible. AI makes this issue more important. When systems begin deciding what to present, how to rank options, what question to ask next, what to recommend, or what action to take based on a prediction, the observed demand that companies ultimately see may already contain the influence of the system itself. How much of the demand we observe reflects what the customer already needed, and how much emerged through the interaction itself? Figure 1. The full mechanism of demand formation. 1. We Have Treated the "Arrow" as Too Simple Suppose a customer chooses Product A from three options. The intuitive conclusion is straightforward: The customer chose A, so A must best reflect their preference. But before making that inference, there is another question: Why did this customer see these three options in the first place? In the age of recommendation systems, different customers are rarely shown identical choices. A system may use previous behavior, income, browsing history, search activity, and other signals to determine which products are most relevant to present. The real process may therefore look more like this: The system evaluates the customer → determines which options the customer sees → the customer chooses from those options. In 2021, researchers from Cornell and Stanford described this problem in a paper titled "Choice Set Confounding in Discrete Choice." Many preference models infer what people prefer from the choices they ultimately make. But the choice set itself may already depend on the chooser's characteristics and existing preferences. Recommendation systems are a classic example. If that mechanism is ignored, two different things can easily become mixed together: What the customer already preferred, and what the system chose to place in front of them. The hotel-booking example in the study makes this easy to understand. Suppose a recommendation system has already filtered hotels based on a user's preferences, and the user consistently chooses the cheapest hotel among those presented. A model might conclude that price is the dominant factor in that person's preference. But that conclusion may overstate the importance of price. Location, star rating, or other attributes may already have been filtered earlier in the recommendation process. Once researchers accounted for this confounding, price became less dominant, and other factors became more important. Preference is not the same as underlying need. But choices and expressed preferences are important behavioral signals companies use to infer what customers need. That means demand discovery cannot focus only on what the customer ultimately chose. It must also consider the choice environment in which that decision was made. 2. AI Does Not Just Influence What We See. It Can Change What We Choose. Choice set confounding tells us that a final choice cannot be understood independently of the options that preceded it. But there is an even more direct question: Can AI recommendations themselves change what people choose? A 2026 Pension Portfolio Experiment posted on arXiv provides a clear example. Researchers recruited 400 South Korean employees who were actually enrolled in workplace defined-contribution pension plans. In a simulation, participants first allocated a hypothetical pension balance across 11 investment products. They were then randomly assigned one of two AI-generated recommendations: one relatively aggressive and concentrated, the other relatively conservative and diversified. Participants could then revise their original portfolios. Three findings stand out: 81% changed their portfolios after receiving the AI recommendation. Among those who revised, 95% moved in the direction suggested by the AI. The difference between the two AI recommendations was partially transmitted into the final portfolios: the resulting difference between the two participant groups was about 37% as large as the original difference between the recommendations. In other words, people did not simply follow the AI wholesale. But different AI recommendations still produced different final decisions. The effects went beyond superficial portfolio changes. Participants who received the more aggressive recommendation ended up with higher expected returns and volatility, less exposure to low-risk products, and more exposure to high-risk products. The study did not find a significant improvement in risk-adjusted performance, but AI clearly changed the risk structure participants ultimately accepted. The important point is the causal relationship: Different AI recommendations produced different final choices. Participants still retained much of their original judgment. The final decision was therefore neither purely human nor purely AI-generated. It emerged from the interaction between the two. Now consider what happens next. If a company later observes those revised portfolios and records them as new evidence of "customer preference," that data already contains some of the influence created by the AI itself. At that point, saying "The customer chose A, therefore the customer prefers A" is no longer a sufficient inference. 3. When a Model Begins to Influence the World It Will Later Observe This leads to another important idea: Performative Prediction. In 2020, researchers at UC Berkeley used this term to describe situations in which a prediction, once used to support a decision, changes the very outcome being predicted. Consider a simple credit example. A bank predicts that a borrower has a high probability of default and therefore charges a higher interest rate. But the higher interest rate increases the borrower's repayment burden, which may itself increase the probability of default. The sequence becomes: Prediction of high default risk ↓ Higher interest rate ↓ Actual default risk changes The model appears to describe the world, but once deployed, it also begins to influence the world it is describing. Similar dynamics can occur in traffic prediction, policing, recommendation systems, and financial markets. Applied to demand discovery, the mechanism might look like this: The model predicts that a customer may need A ↓ A is shown more prominently ↓ A is recommended ↓ The interaction increasingly centers on A ↓ The customer ultimately chooses A At this point, the first layer of influence has already occurred: AI has affected the customer's choice. The pension experiment shows that this can happen in practice. But there is a second layer. If the company then uses that choice as training data for the next generation of its model: The customer chooses A ↓ The system records "customers like this prefer A" ↓ Similar customers are more likely to be shown A in the future The company is no longer merely observing demand. It is beginning to participate in the formation of the demand it will later observe. This does not mean the model is necessarily wrong. The problem arises when companies forget that their own ranking, recommendation, and interaction mechanisms have already entered the causal process. They may then treat outcomes partly produced by the system as if they were pure evidence of the customer's original preferences. 4. The Path From Underlying Need to Observed Demand Is a Formation Process The apparently simple relationship: Underlying Need → Observed Demand can therefore be expanded into something closer to this: Underlying Need ↓ Customer Expression ↓ AI Interpretation ↓ Option Configuration / Recommendation ↓ Interaction / Intervention ↓ Customer Reassessment ↓ Observed Demand Several mechanisms operate inside this process. Choice architecture: determines what the customer sees and how alternatives are arranged. Interaction: determines how the system asks, responds, and continues the conversation. Recommendation: introduces new information and direction into the customer's judgment. Intervention: occurs when the company acts on the model's judgment in ways that affect subsequent responses or decisions. None of these mechanisms is entirely new. What AI changes is its scale, personalization, speed, and ability to operate continuously. There is also an important distinction to make. The fact that demand is shaped through interaction does not necessarily mean it is being distorted. In many real situations, customers themselves may not fully understand what they need at the beginning. A well-designed discovery process can use questions, comparisons, and different scenarios to help customers clarify what they actually value. The interaction therefore has two simultaneous functions. On one hand, it generates new signals and reduces uncertainty about the underlying need. On the other hand, the way questions are asked, options are presented, and recommendations are made can also influence how customers think and respond. In the past, demand discovery was easier to think of primarily as a form of measurement. With AI, measurement and intervention increasingly occur at the same time. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate intervention altogether. It is to distinguish between signals that reflect a relatively stable underlying need and signals that were caused by a particular question, choice set, or recommendation. 5. From Collecting Answers to Identifying Causes If a company relies mainly on correlation, the logic is straightforward: The customer chose A → therefore the customer needs A. But once the system itself has participated in presenting, recommending, and explaining A, that inference becomes less reliable. The more important question becomes: If the conditions were different, would the same need still appear? Would the customer still choose A if A had not been recommended first? If the price changed, would the customer still value the same type of protection? If the customer saw a different set of alternatives, would the expressed preference remain? If family responsibilities changed, would the need for protection change as well? These are fundamentally counterfactual questions: If a particular condition had been different, would the outcome also have been different? The contrast can be summarized as a shift from a traditional approach based on observed behavior and correlation to a causal approach that varies conditions and interventions to test demand hypotheses. By introducing different conditions and interventions, companies can test competing demand hypotheses. Some changes should theoretically have little effect on a genuine underlying need. Other causal factors, when changed, should produce corresponding changes in demand. When customer responses behave consistently with these causal hypotheses, companies have stronger grounds for believing they are identifying the underlying need rather than merely predicting an observed response. The choice set confounding research points in the same direction. When companies understand the variables used to assign choice sets and the mechanism by which those choice sets were generated, causal methods such as inverse probability weighting and regression controls can help reduce confounding and recover preferences more accurately. AI therefore does not make genuine customer needs impossible to understand. But it changes what understanding requires. Companies cannot simply accumulate more behavioral data and expect the truth to emerge automatically. They need to understand the conditions under which each signal was generated, and whether the signal still holds when those conditions change. A more mature AI demand-discovery process therefore cannot stop at: Ask questions → collect answers → predict demand It also needs to: Form a demand hypothesis ↓ Design appropriate questions and scenarios ↓ Observe responses under different conditions ↓ Control for possible confounding ↓ Continuously revise the judgment of the underlying need For example, a customer may ultimately choose Product A for very different reasons: The customer genuinely needed A from the beginning. The system placed A in front of the customer first. The system repeatedly recommended A. The way the questions were framed directed the customer's attention toward A. Other relevant alternatives were never presented. The observed choice may look identical in every case, but the mechanism that produced it is not. Interaction is therefore no longer just a way to collect more data. Every interaction can also become a test of a demand hypothesis. The goal is therefore not simply to improve the predictive accuracy of observed demand. It is to improve the company's causal ability to identify underlying need. Conclusion: Put the Company Back Into the Causal Chain Traditionally, the challenge of demand discovery has been to look beyond surface-level statements and choices to understand what customers actually need. AI adds a layer. Once a system begins participating in option design, recommendation, questioning, and decision-making, the observed demand that a company sees may already contain the influence of its own AI. Companies can therefore no longer ask only: How do we infer underlying need from observed demand? They must also ask: Through what mechanism was this observed demand produced? And once measurement and intervention can no longer be cleanly separated, companies need more than stronger predictive models. They need causal methods that can continuously improve their ability to identify underlying needs while interacting with and influencing customers. A mature AI demand-discovery system should incorporate intervention into its design so that every question, option, and interaction helps distinguish among three things: what the customer already needed, what the system itself helped cause, and what became clearer through the interaction. If companies want to understand demand in the AI era, they must begin by putting themselves back into the causal chain. David Lien

The sequence becomes: Prediction of high default risk ↓ Higher interest rate ↓ Actual default risk changes The model appears to describe the world, but once deployed, it also begins to influence the world it is describing. Similar dynamics can occur in traffic prediction, policing, recommendation systems, and financial markets. Applied to demand discovery, the mechanism might look like this: The model predicts that a customer may need A ↓ A is shown more prominently ↓ A is recommended ↓ The interaction increasingly centers on A ↓ The customer ultimately chooses A At this point, the first layer of influence has already occurred: AI has affected the customer's choice. The pension experiment shows that this can happen in practice. But there is a second layer. If the company then uses that choice as training data for the next generation of its model: The customer chooses A ↓ The system records "customers like this prefer A" ↓ Similar customers are more likely to be shown A in the future The company is no longer merely observing demand. It is beginning to participate in the formation of the demand it will later observe. This does not mean the model is necessarily wrong. The problem arises when companies forget that their own ranking, recommendation, and interaction mechanisms have already entered the causal process. They may then treat outcomes partly produced by the system as if they were pure evidence of the customer's original preferences. 4. The Path From Underlying Need to Observed Demand Is a Formation Process The apparently simple relationship: Underlying Need → Observed Demand can therefore be expanded into something closer to this: Underlying Need ↓ Customer Expression ↓ AI Interpretation ↓ Option Configuration / Recommendation ↓ Interaction / Intervention ↓ Customer Reassessment ↓ Observed Demand Several mechanisms operate inside this process. Choice architecture: determines what the customer sees and how alternatives are arranged. Interaction: determines how the system asks, responds, and continues the conversation. Recommendation: introduces new information and direction into the customer's judgment. Intervention: occurs when the company acts on the model's judgment in ways that affect subsequent responses or decisions. None of these mechanisms is entirely new. What AI changes is its scale, personalization, speed, and ability to operate continuously. There is also an important distinction to make. The fact that demand is shaped through interaction does not necessarily mean it is being distorted. In many real situations, customers themselves may not fully understand what they need at the beginning. A well-designed discovery process can use questions, comparisons, and different scenarios to help customers clarify what they actually value. The interaction therefore has two simultaneous functions. On one hand, it generates new signals and reduces uncertainty about the underlying need. On the other hand, the way questions are asked, options are presented, and recommendations are made can also influence how customers think and respond. In the past, demand discovery was easier to think of primarily as a form of measurement. With AI, measurement and intervention increasingly occur at the same time. The challenge is therefore not to eliminate intervention altogether. It is to distinguish between signals that reflect a relatively stable underlying need and signals that were caused by a particular question, choice set, or recommendation. 5. From Collecting Answers to Identifying Causes If a company relies mainly on correlation, the logic is straightforward: The customer chose A → therefore the customer needs A. But once the system itself has participated in presenting, recommending, and explaining A, that inference becomes less reliable. The more important question becomes: If the conditions were different, would the same need still appear? Would the customer still choose A if A had not been recommended first? If the price changed, would the customer still value the same type of protection? If the customer saw a different set of alternatives, would the expressed preference remain? If family responsibilities changed, would the need for protection change as well? These are fundamentally counterfactual questions: If a particular condition had been different, would the outcome also have been different? The contrast can be summarized as a shift from a traditional approach based on observed behavior and correlation to a causal approach that varies conditions and interventions to test demand hypotheses. By introducing different conditions and interventions, companies can test competing demand hypotheses. Some changes should theoretically have little effect on a genuine underlying need. Other causal factors, when changed, should produce corresponding changes in demand. When customer responses behave consistently with these causal hypotheses, companies have stronger grounds for believing they are identifying the underlying need rather than merely predicting an observed response. The choice set confounding research points in the same direction. When companies understand the variables used to assign choice sets and the mechanism by which those choice sets were generated, causal methods such as inverse probability weighting and regression controls can help reduce confounding and recover preferences more accurately. AI therefore does not make genuine customer needs impossible to understand. But it changes what understanding requires. Companies cannot simply accumulate more behavioral data and expect the truth to emerge automatically. They need to understand the conditions under which each signal was generated, and whether the signal still holds when those conditions change. A more mature AI demand-discovery process therefore cannot stop at: Ask questions → collect answers → predict demand It also needs to: Form a demand hypothesis ↓ Design appropriate questions and scenarios ↓ Observe responses under different conditions ↓ Control for possible confounding ↓ Continuously revise the judgment of the underlying need For example, a customer may ultimately choose Product A for very different reasons: The customer genuinely needed A from the beginning. The system placed A in front of the customer first. The system repeatedly recommended A. The way the questions were framed directed the customer's attention toward A. Other relevant alternatives were never presented. The observed choice may look identical in every case, but the mechanism that produced it is not. Interaction is therefore no longer just a way to collect more data. Every interaction can also become a test of a demand hypothesis. The goal is therefore not simply to improve the predictive accuracy of observed demand. It is to improve the company's causal ability to identify underlying need. Conclusion: Put the Company Back Into the Causal Chain Traditionally, the challenge of demand discovery has been to look beyond surface-level statements and choices to understand what customers actually need. AI adds a layer. Once a system begins participating in option design, recommendation, questioning, and decision-making, the observed demand that a company sees may already contain the influence of its own AI. Companies can therefore no longer ask only: How do we infer underlying need from observed demand? They must also ask: Through what mechanism was this observed demand produced? And once measurement and intervention can no longer be cleanly separated, companies need more than stronger predictive models. They need causal methods that can continuously improve their ability to identify underlying needs while interacting with and influencing customers. A mature AI demand-discovery system should incorporate intervention into its design so that every question, option, and interaction helps distinguish among three things: what the customer already needed, what the system itself helped cause, and what became clearer through the interaction. If companies want to understand demand in the AI era, they must begin by putting themselves back into the causal chain. David Lien

items.extracted_text: USAA lifts Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond target to $350m as price guidance drops - Artemis.bm USAA lifts Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond target to $350m as price guidance drops - Artemis.bm USAA lifts Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond target to $350m as price guidance drops 21st October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans USAA is aiming to upsize its latest catastrophe bond issuance by 56% and secure the protection at reduced pricing, as the insurer now targets $350 million of collateralized multi-peril catastrophe reinsurance from the Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) issuance, Artemis understands. The US military mutual insurer returned to the catastrophe bond market earlier this month , with an initial target to secure $225 million of multi-year per-occurrence reinsurance coverage from capital market investors with the latest in its Residential Re series of cat bond deals. USAA is still the most consistent and long-standing catastrophe bond sponsor in the marketplace, having added to and diversified its sources of catastrophe reinsurance protection using the capital markets since the beginning of cat bonds back in 1997 and this Residential Re 2026-2 issuance set to become the 48th cat bond for USAA that we have analysed and tracked. You can read about all of USAA’s 47 issuances under the Residential Re name, as well as one named Espada Re cat bond, in our extensive Deal Directory . Being among the first new catastrophe bonds to come to market in the fourth-quarter of 2026, the pricing signal the deal sends speaks to the well-capitalised nature of the market, with cat bond funds having accumulated cash from returns generated through the so-far loss-free US hurricane season. Having launched the deal with a $225 million target issuance size, we’re now told that has jumped 56% to $350 million, while at the same time the price guidance for all three tranches of notes has been lowered. The Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited special purpose vehicle is offering three tranches of Series 2026-2 occurrence catastrophe bond notes to investors, with the proceeds set to be used to collateralize underlying reinsurance agreements between the issuing vehicle and sponsor USAA. Each of the tranches of notes will provide USAA with four years of indemnity per-occurrence based reinsurance protection, running from December 1st 2026 through November 30th 2030, to cover losses from the typical perils that feature across all of the insurers catastrophe bond deals in recent years, being U.S. tropical cyclones, earthquakes (plus fire following), severe thunderstorm, winter storm, wildfire, volcanic eruption, meteorite impact, other perils (all including auto & renter policy flood losses). A Series 2026-2 Class 2 tranche of notes was preliminarily sized at $50 million, but we’re now told target $100 million of protection for USAA. These notes come with an initial base expected loss of 6.04% and were first being offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 8.5% to 9.25%, but we’re now told that guidance has been updated at between a 7.75% and 8.5% spread. What was initially a $50 million Series 2026-2 Class 3 tranche of notes are now targeted also at $100 million in size. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 3.34% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 5% to 5.5%, but sources said the price guidance for this layer has been adjusted down to between 4.25% and 5%. The final Class 5 tranche of Series 2026-2 notes were initially targeted at $125 million in size, but again this has increased to a $150 million target, we understand. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 1.43% and were initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 2.5% to 3%, which has again been reduced to an updated range of between 2% and 2.5%. So all three tranches of catastrophe bond notes from this Residential Reinsurance 2026-2 offering for USAA have increased in size, while their price guidance has been revised to below the initial ranges. In terms of how much price guidance has fallen, from the initial to the new mid-points of the updated ranges, the tranches have seen an 8.5%, 12% and 18% price decline, so on average almost 13% across the three layers of risk on offer to investors. As we said, that speaks to the well-capitalised nature of the catastrophe bond market, as well as to investor appetites for the first new 144A cat bonds to come to market after the hurricane season issuance lull. We imagine the price signals this sends will inform reinsurance buyers and this could begin to attract more issuers to the cat bond market ahead of the end of year renewal season, as it seems the cat bond market is continuing to execute at efficient levels for sponsors. With now 48 catastrophe bond transactions from USAA now detailed in our Deal Directory, the insurer and its now 47 deal strong Residential Re cat bond program is the most prolific sponsor and program in the market, a regular and consistent feature since the cat bond instrument was first seen in late 1996 when USAA’s first began marketing. You can read all about this new Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond from USAA and view details on almost every other cat bond ever issued in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: Hannover Re targets 75% upsized $350m of limit from new Acorn Re parametric cat bond - Artemis.bm Hannover Re targets 75% upsized $350m of limit from new Acorn Re parametric cat bond - Artemis.bm Hannover Re targets 75% upsized $350m of limit from new Acorn Re parametric cat bond 21st October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Hannover Re’s seventh catastrophe bond offering in the annual Acorn Re parametric US earthquake series of deals looks set to grow, as the target size for this issuance has been raised by 75% to now seek $350 million of limit from the Acorn Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) issuance, sources have said. Hannover Re returned to market with this new and now seventh Acorn Re parametric catastrophe bond earlier this month , initially seeking $200 million of risk transfer and reinsurance limit for the single named ceding insurer, Oak Tree Assurance Ltd. while also sourcing additional protection to cover other reinsurance deals it has entered into. These parametric catastrophe bonds, under the Acorn Re series, play a kind of dual role in protecting Oak Tree Assurance, a Vermont-based workers compensation captive insurer of the Kaiser Permanente group of health plan companies, while also providing a type of retrocessional reinsurance for Hannover Re to protect other reinsureds that might face losses under the cat bond’s trigger conditions. Acorn Re parametric earthquake cat bonds have now been issued four years in a row, as this deal becomes an increasingly regular and annual feature of this time of year. Read about all seven Acorn Re issuances in our catastrophe bond Deal Directory . Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (SPI) Acorn Re Ltd. was initially offering a $200 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes to investors, but we’re now told the offering size has been raised 75% to $350 million. The proceeds from the sale of the notes will collateralize underlying retrocessional reinsurance agreements between Acorn Re and Hannover Re and the reinsurer in turn then enters into reinsurance agreements with the Kaiser Permanente captive, Oak Tree Assurance, while also using the protection to cover any losses to its other reinsureds that have exposure in the parametric box. The notes are designed to provide per-occurrence based parametric reinsurance protection against earthquakes that strike the U.S. west coast region, with that protection funded by the capital markets and running across a three year term from November 1st 2026 to the end of October 2029. As with all the previous Acorn Re cat bond deals, the main focus of the parametric reinsurance protection remains earthquakes in California, but the parametric trigger grid or box structure covers neighbouring states as well. The parametric trigger is designed to provide a sliding scale payout structure, meaning different payout percentages are possible depending on the magnitude and location of earthquake loss events, starting at a 25% payout as a minimum. What was initially a $200 million tranche of Acorn Re 2026-1 Class A notes are now sized at $350 million, as we said. The notes have an initial expected loss of 0.78% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 2% to 2.25%, but we’re now told that the price guidance range has narrowed to between 2% and 2.15%. Which represents only a slight price decline, of around 2.4% from the initial to the updated mid-points of spread guidance, but being such a remote risk cat bond deal and with a thin spread from the start, that’s not surprising as investors do have minimum return requirements below which lower-risk cat bond investments just don’t make as much sense. items.extracted_text: PERILS lifts July European convective storms insured market loss estimate to €2.8bn - Artemis.bm PERILS lifts July European convective storms insured market loss estimate to €2.8bn - Artemis.bm PERILS lifts July European convective storms insured market loss estimate to €2.8bn 20th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Catastrophe data aggregator PERILS AG has updated its estimate of insurance industry losses for the severe convective storms (SCS) that swept across Germany, France, Switzerland, and Italy in Europe between July 13th and 19th, 2026, lifting the total to EUR 2.806 billion. The storms are also known as “SCS Cerry”, following the naming of an associated low-pressure system by the Free University of Berlin. PERILS published its initial industry loss estimate for the severe convective storms in late August, putting the total at EUR 2.186 billion. As we said at the time, this outbreak of severe convective storms (SCS) across Europe became the largest loss from that peril in Europe in the PERILS AG list of loss events. It also marked the largest insurance industry loss estimate for any European catastrophe event that PERILS has issued since the series of European windstorms in February 2022. Now in its second industry loss estimate from the event, PERILS has lifted the total by roughly 28% to EUR 2.806 billion. PERILS explained that its loss estimate is based on data gathered from impacted insurers, including losses from property and motor lines of business. PERILS will also publish a third estimate of the market loss from the mid-July severe convective storms on January 19th, 2027, six months after the event end date. Earlier this week, PERILS also published its initial loss estimate for the severe convective storm and hail outbreak that struck parts of western Europe between August 26th and 28th 2026, placing the total at EUR 3,296 million. This event, combined with the July outbreak, showcases how costly European SCS activity has been in recent months. At the same time, CatIQ, Canada’s insured loss and exposure indices provider and subsidiary of PERILS, has published its second industry loss estimate for the severe convective storms that struck southern Ontario, including Toronto, on September 2nd and 3rd, 2026, lifting the total to CAD $671 million. CatIQ published its initial loss estimate from the event earlier this month, putting the total at $563 million. With claims having continued to be filed, the total has risen steadily now, increasing by roughly 19% to $671 million for the second industry loss estimate. CatIQ’s loss number covers both property and motor lines of business. The company also confirmed that it will publish its third loss estimate of the market loss from the southern Ontario SCS on December 3rd, 2026, three months after the event end date. Luzi Hitz, Product Manager at PERILS, commented: “These two loss updates show clearly that severe convective storms are a major risk for the insurance markets in Europe and Canada. In fact, in recent years most mid-latitude countries globally have experienced more severe losses from convective storms than previously. “There are multiple factors driving this. Firstly, this reflects the increase in vulnerable assets such as solar panels, roof windows, light-weight blinds and soft external wall insulation. Also, as economies grow there are simply more assets at risk of damage. Finally, the warming climate is driving an increase in the formation of more violent and damaging SCS events.” Caroline Floyd, Director of CatIQ, said: “Severe convective storms have again been at the forefront of what has been a very active year for Canadian catastrophes. More than half of the year’s events involved SCS, including multiple major catastrophes affecting large population centres. items.extracted_text: After the heatwaves: how risk manages should prepare for an uncertain nat cat future - Commercial Risk Flooding in the Emilia-Romagna region Europe’s summer heatwaves may have faded from the headlines, but the risk environment they revealed has not. Consequently, says BELFOR’s Martin Schachtschneider*, risk managers face a future in which yesterday’s loss scenarios, historical statistics and recovery assumptions may no longer provide a reliable guide to tomorrow. Italy experienced an exceptional summer of extreme weather with temperatures soaring to record-highs. Successive heatwaves and severe droughts led major commercial waterways like Lake Maggiore and the Po River to experience plummeting water levels – causing crop failures and disruption to cargo shipping, hydroelectric generation and cooling operations for power plants. However, as the summer faded and the heatwaves and wildfires subsided, Italian companies were paradoxically faced with a barrage of rainfall and potential floods. September saw a series of massive convective storms across Northern and Central Italy, including 40,000 lightning strikes recorded in Liguria in 24 hours and a collapsed bridge in Sonico. And in October, extreme rainfall from the likes of Storm Adam have caused widespread disruptions and closures. Things could get worse still because El Niño, the global climate phenomenon caused by variations in winds and sea surface temperature, is back and is forecast to be exceptionally strong. The last El Nino phase that started in 2023 led to the hottest year on record – in 2024, temperatures were almost 1.5 degrees above the pre-industrial average. It is therefore possible that 2027 could exceed those temperature levels. This does not automatically dictate that there will be unprecedented levels of rainfall all over Europe. But it will lead to increased weather volatility and greater uncertainty that won’t be captured in traditional risk models. As Munich Re states: “Using historical statistics alone for risk management is not enough. Instead, fluctuations from natural climate cycles need to be considered, and the long-term effects of climate change precisely mapped in the risk strategy.” Even with updated models, risk managers will find it harder to predict or control their losses in such volatile conditions. But if we look at the traditional sequence of events following a natural catastrophe – loss event > damage > business interruption > recovery > restart – there is one part that can be easily optimised – the recovery. For many companies caught in a natural disaster, insurance is not the immediate issue, it is about recovery and restoration and ensuring there are providers on hand to help. However, when disaster hits, the contractors that specialise in disaster recovery find their order books filled over night as they are inundated with emergency calls – no tenders or bidding rounds or beauty contests are involved at this stage. Companies are not just looking to recover their facilities, they are fighting to survive. Unfortunately, some companies have lost this battle. Those companies in need but without a contracted supplier have had to wait, sometimes weeks. Even simple tasks like pumping out basements or removing screed were delayed. In this time, moisture can seep in deeper, mould grows, corrosion eats through equipment and the damage is compounded day by day. To avoid falling for the availability illusion, risk managers need a realistic picture of resource availability for every location domestically and international. And most importantly, companies have to ensure they have contractually secured the services of a partner with the capacity and expertise needed at a time of emergency and who can guarantee to arrive first in the event of a major disaster. BELFOR’s RED ALERT® service provides clients with contracted priority and has proved invaluable to companies in their time of greatest need by ensuring they are at the front of the line when disaster hits. “In Italy, one of our sites was badly affected by the 2023 floods,” says Matthias Beck, head of insurance and risk management at German industrial distributor Würth Group. “When the phone rang, I was able to reassure my colleagues immediately: BELFOR is coming. They have the necessary resources and know Würth. Würth is a RED ALERT® customer and, therefore, enjoys priority status.” For over 50 years, BELFOR has helped companies minimise business interruption following disasters and we have repeatedly seen how smart risk management can make the difference. The next catastrophe may be a flood, a storm, a wildfire or an event that has never affected your region before. Risk managers do need to challenge the assumption that, once it happens, help will simply be available to minimize downtime after a loss. In the new Nat Cat reality, resilience starts before the event, and availability must be secured before everybody needs. The Availability Illusion is only one of nine costly pitfalls that businesses often overlook before a major loss. Download BELFOR’s latest report here for corporate and risk managers to identify the 8 other blind spots that could slow down your recovery when every hour matters after a major loss. *Martin Schachtschneider, Head of Corporate Client Solutions, BELFOR.
